summary: Provides the network management framework for the MPLS Transport Profile, using ITU-T management terminology. It describes network and element management architectures and ideas for fault, configuration and performance management. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lays out how an MPLS transport network should be managed: how the management systems are arranged, and what the network equipment has to be able to do about faults, configuration and performance. It borrows its vocabulary from the ITU, so it is heavier going than most.

questions: how should mpls-tp networks be managed
what are the main management functions in mpls-tp
subtitle: How an MPLS transport network should be managed: the architecture, and what the equipment has to do about faults, configuration and performance.

tldr.problem: MPLS transport networks need a management architecture that covers the whole network and the equipment in it, without assuming any particular management protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a multi-tiered management network, the management functions inside each network element, and the ITU-T approach to fault, configuration and performance management.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol and fixes no vocabulary, but it sets out how the management plane and the control plane divide ownership of a path and how they hand it over.

facts.label: Ownership handover required
facts.value: From the Management Plane to the Control Plane

today: RFC 5950 is an Informational document published in September 2010, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a framework rather than a specification: it fixes no protocol and no vocabulary, and it points to other documents for the requirements, the signalling extensions and the security framework.

sections.title: What This Framework Covers
sections.content:
This document gives the network management framework for the Transport Profile for Multi-Protocol Label Switching, MPLS-TP. The requirements for network management in an MPLS-TP network are in a separate document, and this one explains how network elements and networks that support MPLS-TP can be managed using solutions that satisfy those requirements. The relationship between operations, administration and maintenance, management and the other framework documents is described in the MPLS-TP framework document.

The framework leans on ITU-T management terminology to describe the architecture that could be used for an MPLS-TP management network. The terms come from ITU-T G.7710, G.7712 and M.3013, and the vocabulary is dense. A Communication Channel is a logical channel between network elements that can carry management plane or control plane applications; for MPLS-TP the physical channel supporting it is the Management Communication Channel. The Data Communication Network is the network that carries the layer 1, 2 and 3 traffic of distributed management communications, distributed signalling and other operations communications such as order-wire voice calls and software downloads. The part of it that carries management information is the Management Communication Network, and the part that carries signalling is the Signaling Communication Network. An Equipment Management Function holds the management functions inside a network element. A Local Craft Terminal is an out-of-band device that connects to a network element for management. A Management Application Function is an application process that takes part in system management. The Message Communication Function is the communications process that does information interchange and relay. The Network Element Function is the set of functions needed to manage a network element. The Operations System is a system that performs the functions supporting operations, administration, maintenance and provisioning, including the surveillance and testing functions that support customer access maintenance.

For MPLS-TP the effort, the term OAM means the set of tools made of operation activities that keep the network running, administration activities that track resources and how they are used, and maintenance activities that facilitate repairs and upgrades.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC lays out how an MPLS transport network should be managed: how the management systems are arranged, and what the network equipment has to do about faults, configuration and performance.

sections.title: The Management Architecture
sections.content:
The management of the MPLS-TP network could be based on multi-tiered distributed management systems. Each tier provides a predefined level of network management capability. The lowest tier holds the MPLS-TP network element that provides the transport service, and the Operations System at the element management level. The Management Application Function inside the network elements and the Operations Systems provides the management support, and at each entity it can include agents only, managers only, or both. A function that includes managers can manage an agent in another one. Communication to peer network elements and Operations Systems is provided by the Message Communication Function in each entity, and the user reaches the management of the transport network through a Local Craft Terminal attached to a network element or a workstation attached to the Operations System.

A transport management network may consist of several transport-technology-specific management networks. The MPLS-TP one is called an MT.MN, and it can be partitioned into MPLS-TP Management SubNetworks for scalability, such as geography or load balancing, or for administration, such as operation or ownership. The subnetwork can be connected to other parts of the management network through Local Craft Terminals or Operations Systems. Several addressable MPLS-TP network elements may sit at one physical location, and the link between them is normally provided by the communication channels; within a site they may talk over an intra-site channel or over a LAN.

At the element level, the Equipment Management Function is what a management system uses to manage the network element. It exchanges management information with the element's transport functions across management point reference points, and it may contain functions that reduce the data arriving across those reference points. It includes date and time, the FCAPS functions of fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security management, and control plane functions, and it provides event message processing, data storage and logging. The management agent inside it converts internal management information signals into management application messages and back again, and responds to messages from the Message Communication Function by performing operations on the managed objects in a Management Information Base. The Message Communication Function holds the communications functions for the world outside the element: the date and time source, the management plane, the control plane, the local craft terminal and local alarms.
sections.plainLanguage: The management is split into tiers, from the operator's own screen down to the equipment in the street. Each piece of equipment has a small management function inside it, and a communications function that links it to the rest of the management network.

sections.title: Fault Management
sections.content:
A fault is the inability of a function to perform a required action, and does not include an inability caused by preventive maintenance, a lack of external resources, or planned actions. Fault management provides the mechanisms to detect, verify, isolate, notify and recover from the fault.

Supervision is the first step. ITU-T G.7710 lists five basic categories that provide the functionality needed to detect, verify and notify a fault: transmission supervision, quality of service supervision, processing supervision, hardware supervision and environment supervision. Each category provides a set of recommendations to make sure the fault management process is fulfilled.

Validation comes next. ITU-T G.7710 describes a fault cause as a limited interruption of the required function, and it is not reasonable to report every fault cause to maintenance personnel. The validation process turns fault causes, which are events, into failures, which are alarms.

Alarm handling then has to be supported inside the element management system, with mechanisms for severity assignment, alarm reporting control and logging.
sections.plainLanguage: A fault is something that stops a function working, but not planned work or running out of something outside. The RFC follows the ITU's three steps: watch for the trouble, sort the real faults from the noise, and then raise and log the alarms that matter.

sections.title: Configuration Management and LSP Ownership
sections.content:
Configuration management provides the mechanisms to provision the MPLS-TP services, set up security for the services and the network elements, provide the destination for fault notifications and performance parameters, and configure and control operations, administration and maintenance. Hardware and software provisioning and inventory reporting are associated with it as well.

One topic gets its own subsection: LSP ownership handover. An MPLS-TP network can be managed not only by network management systems, on the management plane, but also by control plane protocols. Using the control plane is not a mandatory requirement, but operators often do it to make network configuration and LSP recovery both faster and simpler. Where both planes are present, an LSP can be created by either, and the entity that creates it owns the data plane resources that make it up, so normally only the owner can modify or delete it. That creates the need for the management and control planes to interact so that either can manage all the resources of the network.

An operator may prefer full control of the resources during set-up and then let the network maintain itself automatically through the control plane. That is done by creating the LSPs on the management plane and then transferring ownership to the control plane, which is called ownership handover. Management-plane-to-control-plane handover is a requirement where a control plane is in use that supports it. The reverse, control plane to management plane, is recommended but not required for GMPLS networks, because it has only minor applications, such as moving an LSP from one path to another as a maintenance operation. The handover procedure has already been standardised for GMPLS networks, where the signalling protocol is RSVP-TE, and the RSVP-TE enhancements for it are defined elsewhere.

Interworking between the two planes also covers the exchange of information that the management plane requests, and notifications from the control plane as a result of such a request or of an automatic action such as a failure or an operation. The control plane is asked to report the status of the operations it performs in a reliable way, to offer a way of monitoring the status of control plane objects such as TE link status and available resources, and to log the operations it carries out on control plane LSPs. Logging is one of the most critical aspects, because the management plane always needs an accurate history and status of each LSP and of all the data plane resources involved in it.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things can build a path: the operator's management system, or the network's own control protocol. Whoever builds it owns it, so the RFC explains how to hand a path over from the operator to the network so that it can repair itself.

sections.title: Performance Management
sections.content:
Performance statistics could overwhelm a management network, so flexible instrumentation is needed that gives control over how much performance data is collected. Mechanisms for limiting the quantity of information collected are well known and deployed in IETF standards, such as RMON and its second version, RMON2. The details of the performance data collected, including loss and delay measurement data, are in the network management requirements document.

The RFC distinguishes performance data collected on demand from data collected proactively. On-demand measurement gives the operator the ability to measure performance for maintenance purposes, such as diagnosis or detailed verification of proactive measurement. It is used typically on specific LSP service instances for a limited time, which limits its impact on network performance during normal operation, and so it does not result in scaling issues. Proactive measurement is used continuously over time after being configured with periodicity and storage information, and the data it collects is usually used for verifying the performance of the service. Proactive monitoring has the potential to overwhelm both the process of collecting data at a network element, for any number of service instances traversing it, and the process of reporting that information to the Operations System. Operators would therefore typically limit proactive measurement to a very selective subset of the services being provided, and limit the reporting to statistical summaries rather than raw or detailed statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: Collecting performance data can swamp the management network, so the RFC says to keep the continuous collection to a small set of services and report only summaries, and to use one-off measurements for everything else.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The ability for the authorised network operator to reach the equipment management interfaces when needed is critical to proper operation, so those interfaces need protecting from denial-of-service conditions and from attack. Interfaces that use or access private information should be protected from eavesdropping, from mis-configuration and from mal-configuration by unauthorised network elements, systems or users.

Performance of diagnostic functions and path characterisation involves extracting a significant amount of information about network construction that the operator considers private. The security framework for MPLS and GMPLS networks describes the attacks on the operation and management plane and the background needed to understand security practices in internet service provider environments, and the practices it describes apply to MPLS-TP environments.
sections.plainLanguage: The management interfaces are worth attacking, so they need protection, and the diagnostic tools reveal more about the network than the operator may want to share.
